creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Slot 1 measured this while fixing the flake family and left the decision here.

`bridge_death` waits for a real bridge process to dial the core back:

    load ~30, 20 runs        24ms
    four concurrent gates    12.5s against a 20s allowance, and one outright failure at 20s

That is a process spawn chain starved on a machine roughly eight times oversubscribed, not a deadline two seconds small. It is the one part of the flake family a_2LMQSW9A8 does not explain and its fix does not cure - everything else there was the 500ms snapshot fallback (a_2LO4kETFT), which is fixed.

## Why it is worth a card rather than a shrug

Parallel worktrees are now a normal way of working in this repo, and four agents each reaching a gate at roughly the same time is the expected shape rather than an accident. A test that passes alone and fails in that arrangement teaches an agent to re-run rather than to read, which is exactly what docs/testing.md says a flake costs - and this round proved that cost across four slots (a_2LQZrPHbu).

## There is already a precedent for the answer

`./dev --perf` refuses to run on a machine whose fast cores are committed, on the reasoning that a busy machine there makes the run lie against a checked-in baseline rather than merely slow. The line is a one-minute load average at the performance-core count.

A daemon-backed tier has the same property for a weaker reason: it does not lie against a file, but it does report a failure whose cause is the machine. Worth deciding whether the gate should say so - refuse, warn, or serialize the daemon-backed binaries - rather than leaving each agent to work it out. `./dev --perf --anyway` is the precedent for the escape hatch too.

Not obviously worth building: an integrator can sequence gates by hand, and this round did once it understood the problem. The question is whether that knowledge should live in a person.
title: Four worktrees running the gate at once is a load the suite was never sized for
